notes.meaning: Eliphaz challenges Job to cry out and see if anyone in heaven will take his side. He asks if any of the holy ones—referring to God's angels or faithful servants—would ever support Job's complaints against God. Eliphaz believes no godly being would defend the bitter words Job has spoken.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some traditional Catholic interpreters saw this question as an early reference to seeking the help or intercession of angels and saints in heaven.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz warns that letting anger and jealousy take over will ruin a person. In his view, a foolish man destroys his own life through impatient, bitter complaints against God's choices. He is quietly suggesting that Job's bitter protests prove he is acting foolishly.

Eliphaz shares an example from his own experience of seeing a wicked man seem to prosper and put down deep roots. Yet disaster fell upon that home without warning, showing that God's curse had been on it the whole time. Eliphaz hints that Job's sudden downfall fits this exact pattern.

The children of a foolish man are left defenseless and find no help in the city gate, which served as the public court of law. Without a defender, they are ruined by the fallout of their father's wickedness. This remark cut Job deeply because all of his own children had just died in a sudden disaster.

Desperate, hungry people carry off everything the foolish man harvested, even picking grain caught among the thornbushes. Thirsty raiders swallow up his remaining wealth until nothing is left behind. This pointedly reminded Job of how desert raiders had stripped away his own livestock and crops.

Eliphaz explains that suffering does not sprout out of the ground on its own like a wild weed. Trouble and pain do not arrive by blind chance or simple bad luck. Behind hardship is God's just governing of the world, responding to human wrongdoing.

Trouble belongs to human life as naturally and constantly as bright sparks fly upward from a roaring fire. Because all people inherit a fallen, sinful nature, trials are the common lot of mankind in this world. Eliphaz argues that Job should bear his pain patiently instead of acting surprised by it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase for flying sparks literally means sons of Resheph, which may echo an ancient poetic name for a Canaanite god of fire and pestilence.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz says that if he were in Job's place, he would humbly bring his plea straight to God. Instead of complaining, he would admit his faults and ask the Lord for mercy and restoration. While turning to prayer is good advice, Eliphaz unfairly assumes Job has not already been seeking God.

God is praised as the worker of countless wonders whose greatness cannot be measured or fully understood. His power and wisdom reach far beyond what any human mind can grasp. Because God is so great, people should trust His justice rather than question His ways.

Eliphaz points to falling rain as daily proof of God's gentle, steady power. Showers fall freely from the sky over dry pastures, refreshing the earth and feeding every creature. This gift shows how faithfully God cares for a dry and needy world.

God delights to lift up the lowly and bring sorrowful people into a place of safety. His power turns human fortunes around, raising the poor and brokenhearted out of their misery. Eliphaz shares this truth to urge Job to humble himself so God can restore him.

God shatters the secret plots of tricky people so their clever schemes produce no results. No matter how carefully they plan, they cannot succeed against His will. Human cunning is entirely helpless before the Lord's ruler-ship.

God catches clever schemers in their own traps, causing their sly plans to fall apart completely. The apostle Paul quotes this exact statement in the New Testament to show that worldly wisdom is foolishness to God. The very ditch that evil people dig for others often becomes their own ruin.

Scheming people become so confused under God's judgment that they stumble in broad daylight as if it were midnight. Even in simple, obvious matters, they lose their way and feel around like blind people. God shows that proud human cleverness turns to foolishness without Him.

The Lord steps in to rescue the poor from hurtful words that cut like a sharp sword. He shields the weak from the cruel hands of violent, powerful oppressors. God proves to be the true defender of those who have no earthly helper.

Seeing God protect the helpless gives fresh courage to the weak and downtrodden. At the same time, unjust bullies are silenced in shame when they see their evil plans overturned. God's righteous deliverance takes away every boast from wicked people.

Eliphaz declares that a person is truly blessed when God corrects them, so Job should welcome the Almighty's discipline. Scripture often teaches that a loving Father trains His children through hardship for their own good. However, Eliphaz misjudges Job by assuming this terrible suffering is simply corrective discipline for secret sin.

God may cause a painful wound, but He also bandages it and brings healing. He works like a caring doctor who must cut away sickness in order to restore health. His corrections are never meant to destroy His people, but to lead them to whole life again.

Eliphaz uses a familiar Hebrew poem pattern, speaking of six troubles and then seven, to mean every kind of trial a person could face. God promises to rescue His servants time after time so that evil will not overcome them. No matter how many hardships arrive, the Lord provides complete protection.

God promises to keep His people alive during severe famine and shield them from the sword during warfare. Even when whole nations starve or face violent combat, the Lord has the power to save lives. Eliphaz wants Job to believe that God can easily preserve him through any crisis.

The Lord promises to hide the righteous from slander, gossip, and false accusations that lash like a whip. When disaster breaks out across the land, they will have no reason to be afraid. God's watchful care offers a safe shelter against both cruel tongues and sudden danger.

A person under God's protection can face famine and destruction with calm confidence rather than panic. Even dangerous wild beasts will bring them no dread. This courage comes from knowing that God's shield is stronger than any earthly threat.

Eliphaz paints a picture of nature living in harmony with a faithful person. The stones will not ruin the soil of his fields, and wild animals will live at peace with him. When someone walks in fellowship with God, creation itself seems to support and serve them.

Returning from travel, the godly person finds his tent peaceful, safe, and secure. When he inspects his home and counts his flocks, he discovers that nothing is missing or harmed. Eliphaz holds out this quiet security as the reward of turning back to God.

Eliphaz promises Job that his family will flourish once again if he repents. His children and descendants will grow as plentiful and green as the grass covering the fields. In the ancient world, having a large, healthy family was seen as one of God's greatest earthly gifts.

The upright person will live out a full, ripe life and go to the grave peacefully in old age. He will be gathered home like a sheaf of golden wheat brought to the barn at harvest time. For someone walking with God, death is not a defeat, but a timely journey home after a completed life.

Eliphaz wraps up his first speech by insisting that he and his friends have tested these principles and found them true. He tells Job to listen, learn, and take this advice to heart for his own good. While his general statements about God are true, Eliphaz wrongly applies them to Job's blameless suffering.
